title: Chapter 9 — Education Of Young Women In The United States
paragraphs: No free communities have ever existed without morals; and, as I observed in the earlier part of this work, morals are the work of woman. Consequently, whatever affects the condition of women, their habits, and their opinions, has great political importance in my eyes. Among almost all Protestant nations, young women are far more the mistresses of their own actions than they are in Catholic countries. This independence is still greater in Protestant countries like England, which have retained or acquired the right of self-government; the spirit of freedom is then infused into the domestic circle by political habits and by religious opinions. In the United States the doctrines of Protestantism are combined with great political liberty and a most democratic state of society; and nowhere are young women handed over so early or so completely to their own guidance. Long before an American girl reaches marriageable age, her emancipation from maternal control begins. She has barely ceased to be a child when she already thinks for herself, speaks freely, and acts on her own impulse. The great scene of the world is constantly open to her view; far from being concealed, it is disclosed to her each day more completely, and she is taught to survey it with a firm and calm gaze. So the vices and dangers of society are revealed to her early; she sees them clearly, views them without illusions, and faces them without fear, for she is full of confidence in her own strength, and that confidence seems to be shared by all around her. An American girl scarcely ever displays the virginal bloom amid young desires, or the innocent and ingenuous grace that usually attends the European woman in the transition from girlhood to youth. It is rare for an American woman at any age to display childish timidity or ignorance. Like young women in Europe, she seeks to please, but she knows exactly what pleasing costs. If she does not abandon herself to evil, at least she knows that it exists; and she is remarkable more for purity of manners than for chastity of mind. I have often been surprised, and almost frightened, at the singular skill and happy boldness with which young American women contrive to manage their thoughts and their language amid all the difficulties of a stimulating conversation. A philosopher would have stumbled at every step along the narrow path they trod without accidents and without effort. It is easy to see that, even in the independence of early youth, an American woman is always mistress of herself: she indulges in all permitted pleasures without surrendering to any of them, and her reason never lets the reins of self-guidance drop, though it often seems to hold them loosely.

In France, where remnants of every age are still so strangely mingled in the opinions and tastes of the people, women commonly receive a reserved, retired, and almost cloistral education, as they did in aristocratic times. Then they are suddenly abandoned, without a guide and without help, in the midst of all the irregularities inseparable from democratic society. The Americans are more consistent. They have realized that in a democracy the independence of individuals cannot fail to be very great, youth premature, tastes ill-restrained, customs fleeting, public opinion often unsettled and powerless, paternal authority weak, and marital authority contested. Under these circumstances, believing they had little chance of repressing in women the most vehement passions of the human heart, they concluded that the surer path was to teach her the art of combating those passions herself. Since they could not prevent her virtue from being exposed to frequent danger, they determined that she should know how best to defend it; and they placed more trust in the free vigor of her will than in safeguards that have been shaken or overthrown. So instead of cultivating mistrust of herself, they constantly seek to strengthen her confidence in her own firmness of character. Since it is neither possible nor desirable to keep a young woman in perpetual or complete ignorance, they hasten to give her a precocious knowledge of every subject. Far from hiding the corruptions of the world from her, they prefer that she see them at once and train herself to shun them; and they hold it more important to guard her conduct than to be overly scrupulous about her innocence.

Although the Americans are a very religious people, they do not rely on religion alone to defend the virtue of woman; they seek to arm her reason too. In this they have followed the same method as in several other matters: they first make the most vigorous efforts to bring individual independence to exercise proper control over itself, and they do not call in the aid of religion until they have reached the utmost limits of human strength. I am aware that an education of this kind is not without danger; I recognize that it tends to strengthen the judgment at the expense of the imagination, and to make cold and virtuous women rather than affectionate wives and agreeable companions to man. Society may be more tranquil and better regulated, but domestic life often has fewer charms. These, however, are secondary evils, which can be braved for the sake of higher interests. At the stage we have now reached, the time for choosing is no longer within our control; a democratic education is indispensable to protect women from the dangers with which democratic institutions and manners surround them.
